pedagogy.summary: At 6-7, using structure shifts from noticing a pattern to EXPLOITING it deliberately: reordering 3+9 as 9+3 to count on from the larger number, using place value so 47+10 changes only the tens digit, and seeing that a square is a special rectangle because both have four sides and four right angles. The pedagogy is to make the efficient move and the inefficient move visible side by side, so the child feels why structure pays off — fewer counts, a digit that predictably changes — rather than being told a rule. CCSS MP7 frames this as the step toward the distributive property and flexible use of relationships.
bestPractices: Contrast counting on from the smaller vs the larger addend on the same number line so the child sees three hops beats nine hops and connects that to 'order doesn't change the total'
Use a place-value machine / arrow cards so adding a ten visibly ticks only the tens column, and ask the child to predict which digit will change BEFORE it does
Sort and overlap shape sets (all four-sided, all with right angles) so squares fall inside rectangles, surfacing the structural relationship rather than treating them as separate names
Ask 'is there a quicker way? why does it work?' so the structural strategy is justified, not just performed
keyRepresentations: Number line for count-on-from-larger (comparing hop counts)
Place-value / arrow cards and a tens-and-ones column machine
Venn-style overlapping shape hoops (four sides; four right angles)
Base-ten blocks showing +10 as one added ten-rod
commonMisconceptions: Always counts on from the first number written, not the larger, because order is treated as fixed
Adds 10 by counting in ones or by changing the ones digit (47+10 = 48) rather than seeing the tens digit change
Believes a square is not a rectangle because they look different / have different names (prototype and mutually-exclusive categories)
Applies commutativity to subtraction (34-10 handled like 10-34)

learn.summary: For 6-7 year-olds, using structure shifts from noticing a pattern to deliberately exploiting it: reordering 3+9 as 9+3 to count on from the larger addend, using place value so 47+10 changes only the tens digit, and seeing a square as a special rectangle because both have four sides and four right angles. The core teaching move is to make the efficient and inefficient approaches visible side by side so the child feels why structure pays off — fewer counts, a digit that predictably changes, a shared property — rather than being told a rule, and then justifies why the shortcut is allowed.

activities.title: Choose your start: count on from the larger addend
feedback: If the child says 'both ways are the same / both fine' with no mention of fewer counts, put both counts on one number line so the nine-hop crawl and the three-hop version sit side by side; ask which they'd rather do and why.

If the child insists you must start with the 3 because it is written first, show that starting from 9 still lands on 12, and link the saving to the order-doesn't-change-the-total idea they already know.

If the child reliably picks the larger start for new pairs AND explains it (prompt-free, generalising), extend to larger single-digit pairs; if they can only do it when told 'start from 9', keep comparing hop counts until the choice and reason are their own.
activities.rationale: Comparing hop counts on the same line makes the efficiency payoff felt as the child acts, and ties the shortcut to commutativity instead of presenting it as an arbitrary rule.
sourceClaims: Using structure includes seeing that reordering addends and applying place-value and shape relationships lets students solve efficiently, building toward the distributive property

Pupils should be helped to recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships; manipulatives and representations (e.g. number lines, place-value apparatus) should be chosen to reveal that structure and then faded
learnerActions: For 3 + 9, first count on starting from 3 — draw or hop all nine moves across a number line and watch it crawl from 3 to 12.
Now start from 9 instead and count on three — land on 12 in just three hops.
Say what is the same (both reach 12) and what is different (far fewer hops when you start from the larger number).
Answer: why is swapping the order allowed here? Connect to 'the order you add in doesn't change the total.'
Try the same choice for 2 + 8 and 8 + 2: decide which number to start from and explain your choice before you count.
activities.intendedInsight: Starting the count-on from the larger addend reaches the same total with far less work, and this is allowed because addition can be done in any order (commutativity).

activities.title: Adding ten: predict which digit moves
feedback: If the child adds 10 by changing the ones digit (writing 47 + 10 as 48) or by counting up in ones, return to the ten-rod / tens column: adding one whole ten changes the tens count. Have them predict the column, then check.
Common error to watch for and correct: treating 47 + 10 as 48. The correct result is 57 — only the tens digit increases by one.

If they predict correctly and explain the reason, keep examples within the two-digit range for now (no crossing into the hundreds); a case that crosses into hundreds can come later, once the tens-digit insight is secure.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-check routine with place-value apparatus surfaces the structural reason the tens digit moves, directly confronting the common error of altering the ones digit.
sourceClaims: Using structure includes seeing that reordering addends and applying place-value and shape relationships lets students solve efficiently, building toward the distributive property

Pupils should be helped to recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships; manipulatives and representations (e.g. number lines, place-value apparatus) should be chosen to reveal that structure and then faded
learnerActions: Before adding, predict: when I add 10 to 47, which digit will change and which will stay the same?
Add one ten-rod to a base-ten representation of 47, or move the tens on a place-value / arrow-card setup, and check: the tens change (4→5) and the ones stay the same, giving 57.
Repeat the predict-then-check for 63 + 10, saying which digit changes and why before you do it.
Explain in your own words why adding ten leaves the ones digit alone.
activities.intendedInsight: For two-digit numbers that do not cross into the hundreds, adding ten changes only the tens digit (it goes up by one) because ten is one whole ten; place value, not counting in ones, tells you which column moves.

activities.title: Is a square a kind of rectangle?
feedback: If the child says a square is not a rectangle because they have different names or look different, sort by property so the square lands inside the rectangle set, then name the shared structure.
If the child checks four sides and four right angles to justify the relationship, affirm the property-based reasoning and ask them to find another shape that fits both groups.
Note: the card or paper shapes being sorted are thin physical approximations; focus the child on the mathematical shape represented (its sides and right angles), not on the card itself.
activities.rationale: Sorting and overlapping by property surfaces the structural relationship between squares and rectangles, challenging mutually-exclusive prototype categories.
sourceClaims: Using structure includes seeing that reordering addends and applying place-value and shape relationships lets students solve efficiently, building toward the distributive property

Pupils should be helped to recognise and use mathematical structure and relationships; manipulatives and representations (e.g. number lines, place-value apparatus) should be chosen to reveal that structure and then faded
learnerActions: Sort a mixed set of shapes into groups by property: all shapes with four sides, and all shapes with four right angles.

Overlap the two groups (e.g. two overlapping hoops): the overlap holds every shape with four sides and four right angles, which is the rectangle set. See that squares land there alongside the other rectangles, because they have both properties.
Answer: what is the same about a square and a rectangle, and what is different?
State why a square counts as a special rectangle, pointing to the shared properties rather than the name or how it looks.
activities.intendedInsight: A square is a special rectangle because it has the defining properties of a rectangle (four sides, four right angles); classification should be based on properties, not names or appearance.

activities.title: Does the shortcut still work? Bounding the structure
feedback: If the child applies the swap to subtraction (treats 12 − 4 like 4 − 12), show with objects that you cannot take 12 away from a group of only 4; the order matters for subtraction even though it doesn't for addition.
If the child prefers Maya's way only because '9 is bigger' without mentioning fewer counts or order, prompt them to compare the hop counts and recall why swapping leaves the total unchanged.
activities.rationale: Probing a tuned counterexample reveals whether the child has grasped the structural reason (commutativity of addition) or memorised a surface move, and guards against over-generalising the swap to subtraction.
sourceClaims: Using structure includes seeing that reordering addends and applying place-value and shape relationships lets students solve efficiently, building toward the distributive property
learnerActions: Discuss the diagnostic situation: To work out 3 + 9, Sam started at 3 and counted on nine more; Maya started at 9 and counted on three more. Both got 12. Is one way better, and why?
Say why Maya's way is better (fewer to count on) AND why swapping is allowed (order of adding doesn't change the total).
Test whether the swap idea has limits: does swapping the order also work for 12 take away 4 — could I do 4 take away 12 instead? Explain why not.
Give the general rule you've found: reordering is safe for addition but not for subtraction.
activities.intendedInsight: The reorder-to-the-larger strategy depends on commutativity, which holds for addition but not subtraction; a learner who understands the structure can say where it applies and where it breaks.

constraints: Count-on efficiency should be felt by actually comparing the number of hops for the two starting choices; simply being told 'start from the bigger' performs the move without building the reason.

A scored check or single multiple-choice answer can confirm which start is quicker or which digit changes, but it hides whether the child reasoned structurally or guessed; use it only after the hands-on work and follow with a 'why' question.

Annotated or tap-to-reveal reference pictures (shape hoops, labelled digits) are useful as a reference but do not let the child test the count-on choice or predict a column; they are a scaffold, not the place the strategy is built.
Reordering to count on from the larger addend is justified only for addition; do not let the child extend it to subtraction (12 − 4 is not 4 − 12).
Adding ten changes only the tens digit for two-digit numbers that do not cross into the hundreds; keep examples within that range unless deliberately extending.

Paper/card shape cutouts and base-ten rods are thin physical approximations of ideal figures; direct the child's attention to the mathematical properties (sides, right angles, one whole ten) they represent, not to the physical object.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The original source listed '47 + 10 = 48' as a described misconception (changing the ones digit); the correct answer is 57. The activities teach the correct result and use the 48 error only as the error-to-correct, never as a valid option.

No source claim directly supports the subtraction-boundary move in Activity 4 (that commutativity fails for subtraction); it is a conservative inference consistent with the original's counterexample probe and misconception list, not independently verified.

The original counterexample '12 take away 4 / 4 take away 12' is retained to bound the structure to addition; the rewrite makes explicit that subtraction is not commutative, so the swap must not be applied there.

Non-preferred alternatives from the source (reference-only labelled pictures; a scored check of the structural choice) are preserved as a scaffold reference and a follow-up check in the constraints rather than discarded. The original's 'poor' rating of open dialogue was reframed as a narrow affordance (dialogue without a concrete number line gives nothing concrete to reorder/predict for the visual strategy); Activity 4 still uses dialogue legitimately for bounding/reasoning, and no categorical 'dialogue cannot teach' claim is asserted.

The source's gap/partial/full response levels were folded into activity feedback (prompted vs independent reordering; stating why the tens digit moves; extending when the strategy generalises) rather than stated as a separate rubric.
The '3D adds no structural information' comparative claim and internal prerequisite reteach IDs were omitted; the underlying reteach moves are preserved in feedback.

probeDeeper: Ask 'would you start from the larger number for 2 + 8 as well? what about 8 + 2?' to see if the strategy generalises or was a one-off

Counterexample tuned to this topic: 'you said swapping to start from the bigger number is fine — does that also work for 12 take away 4, can I do 4 take away 12?' to test whether the child bounds the structure to addition
Ask 'which digit changes when I add 10 to 63, and which stays the same? why?' to check the place-value structure is understood, not memorised
Ask 'a square and a rectangle — what is the same about them, and what is different?' to surface property-based rather than name-based classification
assess.correctAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child preferring Maya's way because starting from the larger number means fewer to count on, AND justifying that swapping is allowed because the order of adding doesn't change the total.

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees no reason to prefer either method, or prefers starting from the first-written number, because the strategic value of reordering is not grasped
errorPatterns.nextMove: Put both counts on one number line so the nine-hop crawl and the three-hop version sit side by side; ask which they'd rather do and why, connecting the saving to the commutativity they already know
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says 'they're both the same / both fine' with no reference to fewer counts, or insists you must start with the 3 because it is written first

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds ten by changing the ones digit or counting in ones (47+10 treated as 48 or counted one-by-one), missing that place value fixes which digit moves
errorPatterns.nextMove: Return to base-ten blocks / place-value machine: adding one ten-rod changes the tens count; predict-then-check which column moves
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked to add 10 to a two-digit number, the child alters the ones column or counts singly rather than ticking the tens

errorPatterns.pattern: Insists a square is not a rectangle because they have different names or look different (mutually-exclusive prototype categories)
errorPatterns.nextMove: Sort shapes into overlapping hoops by property (four sides; four right angles) so the square lands inside the rectangle set; name the shared structure
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked 'is a square a kind of rectangle? why?' the child says no on the basis of appearance rather than checking four sides and four right angles

responseLevels.gap: Counts on from the first-written number regardless, adds ten by counting in ones, and classifies shapes by name/appearance; treats each task as separate
responseLevels.full: Independently reorders to count on from the larger, predicts the tens digit will change and says why, and justifies a square as a special rectangle by shared properties — transferring the structural move to new numbers/shapes unprompted
responseLevels.partial: Can carry out the efficient move or state the property when prompted ('start from 9', 'only tens change'), but does not choose it independently or explain why it works

assess.diagnosticPrompt: To work out 3 + 9, Sam started at 3 and counted on nine more. Maya started at 9 and counted on three more. They both got 12. Is one way better than the other? Why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Both children got the right answer, so the number 12 tells you nothing. The discriminating content is WHY one way is better: a child using structure links 'start from the larger' to 'fewer hops' AND to 'order doesn't matter'. A child without it says both are fine or that Sam's is right because 3 comes first.
